title: Paper Straws May Be Worse for Environment than Plastic
paragraphs: In recent years, many cafes and restaurants around the world have replaced plastic straws with paper ones in an effort to protect the environment. However, a new government study in South Korea suggests that paper straws may actually be worse for the environment than plastic in several important ways.

The study was commissioned by South Korea's Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and carried out by the Korean Society for Life Cycle Assessment between May 2025 and April 2026. Its findings were disclosed in October 2026 by Kim Wi-sang, an opposition lawmaker. The researchers compared four types of straws: conventional plastic, paper, biodegradable plastic and bio-based polyethylene, a type of plastic made from plants such as sugarcane. They measured each straw's environmental impact across 16 categories, from the production of raw materials to disposal. The study assumed that about 74% of used straws are burned and 26% are buried in landfills, based on national waste statistics.

Surprisingly, conventional plastic straws had the smallest impact in 10 of the 16 categories, including climate change, particulate matter and human toxicity. In comparison, paper straws scored 6.33 times higher than plastic for their potential to cause cancer in humans, and 2.04 times higher for acidification, a process that can damage soil and water. Bio-based polyethylene straws performed even worse, scoring more than 16 times higher than plastic for cancer-causing impact.

However, it is important to understand what these figures mean. The cancer figure is a calculation based on the entire life cycle of the straws. It does not mean that drinking through a paper straw increases a person's risk of cancer. The results also depend on assumptions about how straws are disposed of.

The researchers also found that straws of all materials are difficult to recycle in practice, mainly because they are so small. As a result, the study recommended that stores should not give out disposable straws automatically, but only when customers ask for them. According to Kim, policy should focus on reducing the overall use of disposable products, rather than simply switching to different materials.
South Korea introduced restrictions on plastic straws in cafes and restaurants in November 2022, but in 2023, the government postponed enforcement indefinitely after complaints from the public.
